outcome: The binary Goldbach conjecture is still unproved: no accepted proof, and no event since 26 Jan 2024 settles it. The window holds (a) a self-published Lean-formalised proof, dated 16 Sep 2026, of a Liouville-valued analogue (every even N > 2 is a + b with λ(a) = λ(b) = -1, summands not required to be prime), which press reports as a GPT-6 Astra result but which the authors' own repository and paper do not credit to any AI system; (b) several analogue, conditional or bound results (Mangerel, Meng, Krishnamoorthy, Zhao, Deligiannis); and (c) a number of unverified self-published claimed proofs.
problem_asks: One universal claim: for every even natural number n > 2 there exist primes p and q with p + q = n. Parts: a single part, the even case over all even n > 2; equivalently, the set of even n > 2 with no such representation is empty. Not asked by this bullet: the odd (ternary) form, which Helfgott settled in 2013 (a separate neighbouring problem); counts of representations as such; the Liouville-valued or other analogues.

events.what_happened: A pseudonymous account, 'Captain Sude' (GitHub CaptainSude, X @captain_sude, one contributor), published the repository CaptainSude/Liouville-Goldbach containing a paper, 'A Goldbach theorem for the Liouville function' (subtitle 'Two commuting symmetries and a descent'), and a Lean 4 / mathlib formalisation. The claim: for every even N > 2 there are positive integers a, b with a + b = N and λ(a) = λ(b) = -1, where λ is the Liouville function (λ(n) = (-1)^Ω(n)). The X announcement could not be opened (HTTP 402 / 451 / redirect). Press reports dated 20-21 Sep 2026 (BlockBeats via ME News and Beating AI; 新智元 via 36Kr and WallStreetCN; a KuCoin flash item; Lookonchain) present it as a result of 'GPT-6 Astra'. The repository, paper and Lean files name no AI system.
events.revisions: Three commits on main, all dated 16 Sep 2026: c1284b1 'Add files via upload', 499f9b3 'Create lean.yml', da3c528 'Create .gitignore'. The AI4Math tracker names da3c528 as the frozen v1.0.0 release and gives 15 Sep 2026 as the candidate date of the X announcement; I could not confirm that date from the post.
events.delivers: Liouville-valued analogue only: for every even N > 2 there are positive integers a, b with a + b = N and λ(a) = λ(b) = -1, i.e. each summand has an odd number of prime factors counted with multiplicity. The Lean docstring and paper state no analytic or conjectural hypothesis. The summands need not be prime, so the result gives no binary Goldbach decomposition. Goldbach implies this statement (every prime has λ = -1), not the reverse.
events.remains: The binary statement for every even N > 2 (both summands prime): the whole of the bullet's question. The odd-N analogues are not asked by this bullet.

events.directly_checkable: The statement, not the proof, can be checked by hand for any given N: e.g. 8 = 3 + 5 with λ(3) = λ(5) = -1; 4 = 2 + 2 with λ(2) = -1. The Lean theorem is short: for even N with 2 < N, there exist positive a, b with a + b = N, liouville a = -1 and liouville b = -1.
events.doubts: (1) Vetting: the paper has no author line and no acknowledgements; the only identified person is the repository owner; I found no journal submission, referee report or written expert assessment as of 10 Oct 2026. (2) AI attribution rests on the announcement and press. The paper, PROOF.md, README and audit repository name no AI system, and the paper does not say how the argument was found; the only authors' statement about AI is the X post, which I could not read. (3) Size and scope differ between reports: WallStreetCN says the first PDF was two pages; a search summary of the X post says 8 pages (unverified); 36Kr's English article says the result covers 'all positive integers divisible by 4'. (4) Inputs: the sister repository CaptainSude/Liouville-Goldbach-Multiples-of-Four describes its Lean proof as 'a checked implication from one explicit published input', Mangerel's Theorem 1.2 (IMRN 2024), supplied as a parameter. The main repository says the complete argument is formalised, and its final theorem takes no hypotheses, but the word Mangerel does not appear in the Lean text I read, so I could not establish whether the main development uses that published bound. (5) The paper credits ideas to others (see people), so 'elementary' describes the route given those inputs.
events.direction: Cuts for the Liouville analogue: it asserts the analogue for every even N > 2. It neither supports nor refutes the binary statement, and its decompositions need not use primes. No counterexample is claimed.
events.object: No counterexample and no explicit witnesses: an existence result for every even N > 2, proved by contradiction. PROOF.md states that the proof 'argues by contradiction': it assumes that for some prime p > 3, 2p has no decomposition into two positive integers both with λ = +1, and derives a contradiction. The stated ingredients are two commuting symmetries, a descent, standard square criteria and quadratic reciprocity. Non-constructive in the sense that it gives no explicit a, b for a given N.
people: Thomas Bloom (credited in the paper for the observation that positive-positive pairs at twice a prime are useful; the README credits a 'scaling observation')
Alexander P. Mangerel (credited for character-like rigidity from missing sign patterns, and for the rigidity and commuting-defect arguments; the sister repository uses his published Theorem 1.2)
Mark Shusterman (credited with posing the question)

systems.name: GPT-6 Astra
systems.what_it_did: Per the announcement as relayed by press, Astra discovered the proof. The relayed sentence (WallStreetCN, attributing to Captain Sude) says Astra proved the 'multiples of 4' case on the first day and on the second day found a new elementary route extending the result to all even numbers greater than 2 (translation: 'According to project author Captain Sude, after Astra proved the multiples-of-4 case on the first day, on the second day it found a completely new elementary proof route that extended the result directly to all even numbers greater than 2!'). The relayed sentence says 'Astra'; the English reports say 'GPT-6 Astra'. The authors' repository does not name any AI system; VibeMathed (not the authors) states 'The AI chose the problem, proved it and then formalized the result in Lean'. The source does not say whether the system was an internal build or a released model.
systems.basis_quote: 据项目作者 Captain Sude 透露，Astra 在第一天证明了「4的倍数」情形后，第二天，它又找到了一条全新的初等证明路线，直接把结果推广到了全部大于2的偶数！

events.what_happened: Lingsen Meng, 'All four Liouville sign patterns occur in the binary decompositions of every integer N ≥ 11' (eScholarship item qt7945n3rh, CC BY 4.0; listed date 24 Sep 2026 per a search result; keywords include formal verification and Lean). Per a search summary of the PDF, the theorem covers N ≥ 2 outside E = {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10} and every sign pair (s, t) in {±1}^2. The paper cites Mangerel's GRH-conditional preprint and 'an anonymous repository' for an elementary, formally verified proof that every even N > 2 has a decomposition with (-1, -1). A VibeMathed entry reports a MathOverflow answer by Meng dated 25 Sep 2026; MathOverflow could not be opened.
events.delivers: Per the search summary (I could read only the PDF's outline, not its abstract): for N ≥ 2 outside E, every sign pair (s, t) in {±1}^2 occurs as a + b = N with positive a, b. Restricted to (-1, -1) this gives the Liouville-valued assertion for even N > 2 outside E. The even N in E that matter here (4, 6, 10) are checked by hand as 2 + 2, 3 + 3, 5 + 5 with λ(2) = λ(3) = λ(5) = -1 (my arithmetic). Analogue only: nothing about prime summands.
events.remains: The binary Goldbach statement, entirely. For the Liouville analogue, the paper's own range leaves nothing open for even N apart from the small cases above, which are checked by hand.
events.doubts: I could not read the abstract or the body text. The PDF's bookmarks show sections including '8. Formal verification' and 'Statement on the use of AI tools'; the text of the AI statement is unknown to me. The paper's (-1, -1) even case depends, by its own citation, on an anonymous repository which it does not verify. Peer-review status and the Lean status of Meng's own formalisation are not established.
events.direction: Sign-pattern analogue; cuts in the direction of the Liouville-valued statement (existence of (-1, -1) pairs). Says nothing against the binary conjecture.

events.what_happened: Alexander P. Mangerel, 'On a Goldbach-type problem for the Liouville function', arXiv:2404.12117 (first submitted 18 Apr 2024). Published in International Mathematics Research Notices 2024(16), 11865-11877 (DOI 10.1093/imrn/rnae149; received 23 Apr 2024, accepted 11 Jun 2024, published 3 Jul 2024, per the publisher page). Proves |Σ_{n<N} λ(n)λ(N-n)| < N-1 for all N ≥ 11, determines the N with no cancellation (N in {2, 3, 5, 10}), and says this answers a question from the 2018 AIM workshop on Sarnak's conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 18 Apr 2024; v2 2 May 2024 (fixed several typos, added a remark); journal version IMRN 2024(16), published 3 Jul 2024.
events.delivers: A bound on the Liouville convolution sum Σλ(n)λ(N-n) for N ≥ 11. This is a correlation of λ, not a count of representations of N as a sum of two integers with λ = -1, and the abstract states no consequence for the existence of such pairs.
events.remains: The binary Goldbach problem entirely; and the existence question for pairs with λ(a) = λ(N-a) = -1 (Shusterman's question), which the abstract does not state as a consequence.

checked_by.who: International Mathematics Research Notices (Oxford Academic), refereed journal
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication 11 Jun 2024 and published 3 Jul 2024, per the publisher page.

events.direction: Correlation bound for the Liouville function; cuts neither way on the Goldbach statement.

events.what_happened: Alexander P. Mangerel, 'On Shusterman's Goldbach-type problem for sign patterns of the Liouville function', arXiv:2412.17199, submitted 23 Dec 2024 (single version at the time I opened it). Assuming the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions (GRH), every sufficiently large even N has a, b ≥ 1 with a + b = N and λ(a) = λ(b) = -1. A second result, under GRH, gives lower bounds on how often each of the four sign patterns of (λ(n), λ(N-n)) occurs when N is a large prime. The proof uses Pierce expansions of n/N.
events.revisions: v1 only, as of my fetch.
events.delivers: Under GRH: the Liouville-valued analogue (λ(a) = λ(b) = -1) for all sufficiently large even N, with no explicit threshold in the abstract. Conditional and analogue; no binary Goldbach content.
events.remains: The unconditional analogue for all even N > 2, and the binary Goldbach statement entirely.
events.direction: Conditional analogue, cutting in the direction of the Liouville-valued statement; no effect on the binary statement.

events.what_happened: Krishnarjun Krishnamoorthy, 'On a conjecture of Corradi and Katai', arXiv:2608.13266 (submitted 13 Aug 2026). The abstract studies Goldbach-type sums of the Liouville function, proves sufficient cancellation in them, and discusses applications to sign patterns of λ.
events.delivers: Cancellation in Liouville Goldbach-type sums (correlations of λ), per the abstract. An analogue; does not count representations of even N by primes. Only the abstract was read.
events.remains: The binary Goldbach statement entirely; the existence statement for (-1, -1) pairs is not stated in the abstract.
events.direction: Analogue correlation result; cuts neither way on the binary statement.

events.what_happened: Genheng Zhao, 'The exceptional set of Goldbach problem and Linnik's constant', arXiv:2511.05631 (v1 7 Nov 2025; v2 23 Jan 2026, current). Proves E(X) = O(X^{7/10}), with ineffective implied constant, where E(X) is the number of even integers below X that are not a sum of two primes. The method also gives P(q) = O(q^5) for the least prime in an arithmetic progression mod q. A search summary attributes the exponent 0.709 to the paper; the v2 abstract says 7/10. I did not open v1.
events.delivers: A power-saving upper bound on the exceptional-set counting function E(X), unconditional per the abstract, with ineffective constant. This moves a quantity the conjecture is about: the conjecture is equivalent to E(X) counting only the number 2 (if 2 is counted) or nothing (if it is not). I did not confirm the paper's convention on whether 2 is counted. The bound says nothing about whether E(X) reaches that conjectured value.
events.remains: Whether the exceptional set is as the conjecture says (empty, or {2}). A bound X^{7/10} with an ineffective constant does not reach any X where the set is known to be the conjectured one.
events.direction: Moves the exceptional-set bound toward the conjecture's expected picture (exceptions are sparse). Neither proves nor disproves the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'A progress on the binary Goldbach conjecture', arXiv:1706.09803, first posted 26 Jun 2017; nine versions, the current v9 dated 13 Mar 2026 ('reformatted and introduction expanded; ideas remain unchanged'). Current abstract: 'As an application we prove conditionally the binary Goldbach conjecture. We develop a series of steps to prove the binary Goldbach conjecture in full. We end the paper by proving the binary Goldbach conjecture for all sufficiently large even numbers.' A 2022 repository record reportedly claims a full proof (search snippet, not opened).
events.delivers: Claimed: every sufficiently large even N (threshold not given in the abstract) is a sum of two primes, stated unconditionally. The full statement is claimed only 'conditionally', and the abstract does not name the condition.
events.remains: All even N below the unstated threshold; the full statement, which the abstract's own wording leaves conditional.
events.doubts: The abstract states the full result only 'conditionally' and does not name the condition. The threshold for 'sufficiently large' is not given. The 2026 revision says the ideas are unchanged since the 2017 version, and I found no expert engagement in nine years.
events.direction: Claims a proof for all sufficiently large even N (partial, if correct); the full statement is claimed only conditionally.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'Lean on Goldbach's Conjecture', EasyChair Preprint 10824. First version 2 Sep 2023 (per a search summary); version 4 dated 6 Sep 2023 on the page I opened. Claims that for even N ≥ 4·10^18 a Lean code verifies an inequality for some m ≥ 11, implying that m is prime, and concludes that 'Goldbach's conjecture is true using the artificial intelligence tools' of Lean 4's mathematics library. A search summary says version 3 fixed Lean code that had returned a proposition instead of a proof.
events.revisions: v1 2 Sep 2023, v2 3 Sep 2023, v3 5 Sep 2023 (fixed Lean code), v4 6 Sep 2023 (per EasyChair version list, via a search summary).
events.delivers: Claimed, for even N ≥ 4·10^18 (beyond the computed range), via an inequality checked in Lean, and then the full conjecture. I did not check the inequality or the Lean code.
events.remains: The whole problem if the claim fails; N ≤ 4·10^18 is covered by computation (Oliveira e Silva, Herzog and Pardi).
events.doubts: EasyChair preprint, not peer reviewed. The abstract's argument turns on an inequality holding for some m. The version history includes a Lean file that returned a proposition rather than a proof (search summary). The phrase 'artificial intelligence tools' refers to Lean's mathlib library, not to an AI system.
events.direction: Claims a full proof; if correct, cuts for the conjecture. Unverified.

events.what_happened: Budee U Zaman, 'Discover a Proof of Goldbach's Conjecture', EasyChair Preprint 13595 (7 Jun 2024, 11 pages). The abstract claims a proof of the full conjecture using 'basic number theory concepts' and 'creative strategies' and says 'more evidence' will follow. The abstract gives no argument and no formal verification.
events.delivers: Claimed full statement (every even n > 2). No proof steps visible on the page I opened.
events.remains: Everything, if the claim fails.
events.doubts: EasyChair preprint, not peer reviewed. The abstract is vague and partly garbled, and the page shows no proof steps.
events.direction: Claims a full proof. Unverified.

events.what_happened: Hristo Nedelchev, 'Final and Rigorous Analytical Proof of Goldbach's Conjecture: Verified Without Errors', Zenodo 14923776 (v1, 25 Feb 2025). Argues via a differential equation with fitted constants (α = 0.1762, b = 1.8298, C = 1.5) and a final formula G(N) = 0.1762 N^1.8298 + 1.5 claimed positive for all even N > 2, with numerical error below 0.04%. Invites peer review.
events.delivers: Claimed full statement; the argument as described rests on fitted constants and numerical tests.
events.remains: Everything, if the claim fails.
events.doubts: Self-published. The constants are fitted to data; numerical agreement cannot establish a statement about all even N. No peer review.
events.direction: Claims a full proof by a method that is numerical fitting as described.

events.what_happened: Pedro Alejandro Chou Rodriguez, 'A simple proof for Goldbach's conjecture', Cambridge Open Engage working paper, posted 27 Nov 2025 (v1 and v2 both dated 27 Nov 2025). The abstract says 'a proof is proposed for Goldbach's conjecture, both for the strong and the weak versions' and calls the conjecture 'absolutely correct'. Only the abstract was readable.
events.delivers: Claimed both strong (binary) and weak (ternary) statements. The argument was not visible to me.
events.remains: Everything, if the claim fails. The weak form is already settled by Helfgott (2013), so the claim's weak part is not new.
events.doubts: The page labels it a working paper not peer reviewed by Cambridge University Press. Only the abstract was read; I found no expert uptake.
events.direction: Claims a full proof. Unverified.

events.what_happened: Taha Muhammad, 'Goldbach Conjecture (Strong) 1st Way', Cambridge Open Engage working paper, v1 11 Nov 2025, v2 10 Feb 2026. The abstract says the paper 'explores a novel constructive approach' to the strong conjecture and states no result.
events.delivers: None stated in the abstract (exploratory).
events.remains: The whole problem.
events.doubts: Working paper, not peer reviewed, and it claims no result in the abstract. Recorded because it presents itself as an approach to the strong conjecture.
events.direction: None stated.

events.what_happened: Nghiem Bao Thinh, 'An Approach Using Combinatorics for the Decomposition of Odd Pairs in Relation to Goldbach's Conjecture', Zenodo 17624323 (v2, 16 Nov 2025). The abstract says 'the problem is solved through a combination of number-theory methods and the pigeonhole principle' and then says 'our results do not set up the Goldbach conjecture'.
events.revisions: v2 (16 Nov 2025); v1 date not seen.
events.delivers: Ambiguous: the abstract says the problem is 'solved' and then says the results do not set up the conjecture. I could read only the abstract.
events.remains: The whole problem on the abstract's own reading.
events.doubts: The abstract contradicts itself on whether the problem is solved. Not peer reviewed.
events.direction: Ambiguous on its own abstract; on the abstract's final statement, it does not settle the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Kenneth A. Watanabe, 'Definitive Proof of Goldbach's conjecture', arXiv:1811.02415 (first submitted 2 Nov 2018; v7 11 Aug 2025). The abstract restricts to even n not divisible by any prime below sqrt(n), argues that the prime-pair count is positive for n > 622 by error analysis, and concludes 'thus proving Goldbach's conjecture'. The abstract says nothing about n ≤ 622.
events.revisions: v2 8 Nov 2018; v3 21 Nov 2018; v4 27 Nov 2018; v5 3 Dec 2018; v6 5 Dec 2018; v7 11 Aug 2025 (per the comments: simplified W(n) function, revised proof, added error analysis and figures). No withdrawal notice.
events.delivers: Claimed full statement via a restricted subset of even n and an error analysis for n > 622, per the abstract. The reduction to the subset, and the range n ≤ 622, are not addressed in the abstract.
events.remains: Everything, if the claim fails.
events.doubts: The abstract addresses a subset of the even numbers and says nothing about n ≤ 622. No peer review or acceptance found. The 2025 revision changed the argument, with no disclosed change to the claim.
events.direction: Claims a full proof. Unverified.

events.what_happened: Redha Bournas, 'The Strong Goldbach Conjecture: Proof for All Even Integers Greater than 362', arXiv:1303.4649 (v1 18 Mar 2013; the abstract says 'we prove that the conjecture is true for all even integers greater than 362'). v2 (5 Sep 2013) is a withdrawal notice with no content: 'The author no longer wishes to publish this paper on the Internet.'
events.revisions: v2 5 Sep 2013, withdrawn (1 KB, no PDF).
events.delivers: Claimed full statement for even n > 362, with the abstract citing verification to 4·10^18 for the rest. Withdrawn by its author.
events.remains: The problem as stated (the withdrawn claim does not change its status).
events.doubts: Withdrawn by its author; v2 has no content.

withdrawn.what: Claimed proof of the strong Goldbach conjecture for all even integers greater than 362 (v1).

events.direction: Withdrawn claim of the full statement.

events.what_happened: Ricardo Barca, 'The binary Goldbach conjecture is also true', arXiv:1207.4802 (v1 18 Jul 2012; 14 versions, current v14 22 Apr 2023). Claims that every even integer greater than 4 is a sum of two primes, deducing this from an explicit estimate of a threshold integer, whose existence the author cites from an earlier paper. The abstract does not say how even integers below the threshold are handled.
events.delivers: Claimed full statement via a threshold argument. The finitely many even integers below the threshold are not addressed in the abstract.
events.remains: Everything, if the claim fails.
events.doubts: The abstract does not cover the finitely many even integers below the threshold. The argument depends on a threshold estimate from an earlier paper, which I did not check. No peer review or uptake found.
events.direction: Claims a full proof. Unverified.

events.what_happened: H. A. Pogorzelski, 'Goldbach Conjecture', Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 292 (1977), pp. 1-12, claiming a proof. Standard references (Shanks, via a search summary; the CRC Mathematics entry) say the proof is not generally accepted. A UMaine news item and a 2012 Boston Globe article report that Pogorzelski still believes he has a proof. The 1977 paper was not accessed.
events.delivers: Claimed full statement. Not verified: the paper was not accessed.
events.remains: Everything, per the references that report non-acceptance.
events.doubts: Standard references report that the proof is not accepted. The author's later claims are reported only in press.
events.direction: Claims a full proof; not accepted per the references I found.

events.what_happened: H. A. Helfgott, 'The ternary Goldbach conjecture is true', arXiv:1312.7748 (v1 30 Dec 2013; v2 17 Jan 2014). Proves that every odd integer greater than 5 is a sum of three primes. The abstract names the binary (strong) conjecture as sharing its 1742 origin, but does not claim it.
events.delivers: The odd (ternary) statement only. A neighbouring problem; nothing about the even statement.
events.remains: The binary statement entirely.
events.direction: Neighbouring problem: settles the odd form, says nothing for the even form.

events.what_happened: Tomás Oliveira e Silva, Siegfried Herzog and Silvio Pardi, 'Empirical verification of the even Goldbach conjecture and computation of prime gaps up to 4·10^18', Mathematics of Computation 83(288), pp. 2033-2060 (2014). The author's bibliography page gives electronic publication on 18 Nov 2013. The paper verifies the even Goldbach conjecture for all even n ≤ 4·10^18 and, via Ramaré and Saouter, the odd Goldbach conjecture up to 8.37·10^26. No arXiv preprint was located.
events.revisions: Earliest dated item found: electronic publication 18 Nov 2013. An earlier preprint or a 2012 GOLDBACH workshop poster may exist; I did not open the poster.
events.delivers: A finite, computer-assisted verification: the even statement holds for every even n ≤ 4·10^18 (sieve computation, not AI). Per §2.1, finitely many instances of a universal claim move nothing; what it establishes is that the exceptional set is empty up to 4·10^18.
events.remains: Every even n > 4·10^18.

checked_by.who: Mathematics of Computation (American Mathematical Society), refereed journal
checked_by.where: https://sweet.ua.pt/tos/bib/4.12.html (the AMS page was not opened)

events.directly_checkable: Not by hand: the result is a computation. The method is a segmented sieve over intervals of length 10^12, as described in the paper (not read directly).
events.direction: Finite verification; consistent with the conjecture up to 4·10^18.

events.what_happened: Theodoros Deligiannis, 'Polynomial correlations of the Liouville function with an application to an additive problem', Zenodo 21581938, version 3 published 26 Jul 2026 (earlier versions not located). As summarised by my fetch tool: an unconditional bound O(X/(log X)^c) for a two-point Liouville correlation; under two stated hypotheses, sufficiently large even N satisfy r(N) ≥ 0.9·C(N)·N(log N)^(-2), reached through a chain of reductions of the binary Goldbach problem; a claim that the Siegel-zero branch is closed unconditionally; computational evidence up to X ≤ 10^10.
events.revisions: v3 (supersedes the previous deposit); earlier versions not located.
events.delivers: An unconditional correlation bound for Liouville; and, under two hypotheses, a lower bound on Goldbach-type representation counts for sufficiently large even N. If the hypotheses were established, the representation-count bound would give the binary statement for sufficiently large N, which is the problem's own quantity; as stated it is conditional and is a reduction chain, not a settlement.
events.remains: The unconditional statement; the two hypotheses; the small-N range; the binary statement for all even N > 2.
events.doubts: Self-deposited. The two hypotheses are not established. The claim that the Siegel-zero branch is 'closed unconditionally' is strong and I did not check it. Computational evidence is limited to X ≤ 10^10.
events.direction: Conditional reduction toward Goldbach-type representation counts; no unconditional settlement.

events.what_happened: Repository CaptainSude/Liouville-Goldbach-Multiples-of-Four, described as 'Conditionally Lean verified proof that every positive multiple of 4 is the sum of two positive integers with Liouville value -1'. Its README says the Lean proof is 'a checked implication from one explicit published input', Mangerel's Theorem 1.2 in IMRN (2024), which is 'supplied as a parameter; its proof is not formalized here', and also says 'The mathematical result is unconditional'. The repository is undated. Press (WallStreetCN, quoting Captain Sude) places the multiples-of-4 case first, on the first day, before the all-even result.
events.delivers: Every positive multiple of 4 is a sum of two positive integers with λ = -1: a Liouville analogue restricted to multiples of 4. The formal result is conditional on Mangerel's Theorem 1.2 as a supplied hypothesis.
events.remains: Even N not divisible by 4 in the Liouville analogue; the binary Goldbach statement entirely.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (version as pinned in the repository README)
machine_checked.note: The README describes a conditional Lean verification. I did not check a sorry claim for this repository.

events.doubts: The formal result depends on a supplied hypothesis, Mangerel's Theorem 1.2, rather than on a formalised proof of that theorem. The README says the mathematics is unconditional and the formal result is conditional; both must be read together.
events.direction: Liouville analogue restricted to multiples of 4; says nothing about primes.
people: Alexander P. Mangerel (published Theorem 1.2 used as input)

events.what_happened: Repository CaptainSude/The-constant-the-curve-and-a-paradox, described as 'A Number Theory dissertation written by Astra and Sol, with minor guidance from Captain Sude'. Title block: 'Sol, Astra and Captain Sude'. Dated 25 Sep 2026, 102 pages. disputes.summary: Press and the announcement credit the Liouville-valued proof to GPT-6 Astra. The authors' repository and paper name no AI system. The AI4Math tracker marks the AI role 'unclear'. VibeMathed states 'The AI chose the problem, proved it and then formalized the result in Lean', which is its own claim. The only authors' statement about AI (Captain Sude's X post) could not be read.

The KuCoin headline calls the result 'Linnik's variant'; 36Kr, the tracker and the repository call it the Liouville version. The statement is the Liouville-valued analogue, not Linnik's theorem on primes plus powers of 2.

The first public claim is dated 15 Sep 2026 (tracker, X), 16 Sep 2026 (repository commits; VibeMathed), and 21 Sep 2026 (press). A search summary also calls a crypto-news item 'September 2025'; the KuCoin page gives 2026-09-21, so that summary's year is wrong.

The size and scope of the Liouville claim differ across reports: a two-page first PDF (WallStreetCN); 8 pages (a search summary of the X post, unverified); 'all positive integers divisible by 4' (36Kr English), which matches the sister repository rather than the main one.

36Kr cites arXiv 2404.12117 for the GRH-conditional result, which is in arXiv 2412.17199. The tracker notes the press conflated the two Mangerel papers. 2404.12117 is the unconditional convolution bound; 2412.17199 is the GRH result.

The repository and paper credit Thomas Bloom (positive-positive pairs at twice a prime; a 'scaling observation') and Alexander Mangerel (rigidity and commuting-defect arguments; the published Theorem 1.2 used as input in the sister repository). No claim of priority by either was found; I did not read Bloom's own posts.

summary: The binary Goldbach conjecture has no accepted advance in the window. The most consequential event is the Liouville-valued analogue published by 'Captain Sude' on 16 Sep 2026 (a paper and a Lean 4 / mathlib formalisation, with a sorry-free claim per the authors' logs, and a clean replay by a third party). It proves that every even N > 2 is a + b with λ(a) = λ(b) = -1. This is a different statement: it does not require prime summands, and Goldbach implies it rather than the reverse, so it neither proves nor refutes the bullet. Press (36Kr, WallStreetCN, KuCoin, Lookonchain, all citing the announcement) reports it as a GPT-6 Astra result and says Astra found the argument; the repository, paper and Lean files name no AI system, the tracker marks the AI role 'unclear', and the only authors' account (the X post) was unreadable. I therefore record the 'GPT-6 Astra' attribution as press-relayed, not as the authors' own statement. Meng's 24 Sep 2026 eScholarship paper proves a broader sign-pattern theorem that includes this (-1, -1) case, but it cites the anonymous repository for the even case and I could read only its outline, so it adds no independent check. Two other events bear on the quantity the conjecture is about. Zhao (Nov 2025; revised Jan 2026) bounds the exceptional-set count E(X) by O(X^{7/10}) with an ineffective constant; that moves a count the statement is about, but the conjectured value is not reached. Deligiannis (Jul 2026) gives a conditional lower bound on Goldbach-type representation counts for large N under two hypotheses. Analogue and conditional results also include Mangerel (2024, GRH-conditional Liouville Goldbach; 2024, a Liouville convolution bound), and Krishnamoorthy (Aug 2026). Other claimed proofs are self-published and unreviewed (Zaman 2024, Nedelchev 2025, Chou Nov 2025, Nghiem Nov 2025, Watanabe 2018 with a 2025 revision, Agama 2017 revised Mar 2026, Vega 2023, Bournas 2013 withdrawn, Barca 2012, Pogorzelski 1977 not accepted). The record also includes a Captain Sude repository that credits 'Astra and Sol' with co-writing a number theory text that explicitly does not solve the conjecture. The OpenAI Astra ten-result announcement of Aug 2026 does not include Goldbach. No AI result on the binary statement was found; searches for Claude, Gemini, AlphaProof, AlphaEvolve and Aristotle returned nothing on it. The judging pass should note that the Liouville claim is the only Lean-formalised event in the window, that its AI attribution rests on press, and that Zhao's bound is the closest event on the conjecture's own counted quantity.
competing_reading: A reader who takes the authors' Lean-verified repository at face value, and the press account that Astra found the argument, could count the September 2026 result as a major AI-assisted advance on the Goldbach family. For this bullet, the case against is that the statement is a Liouville analogue, implied by Goldbach and not implying it. On the exceptional-set count, a reader could treat Zhao's bound as partial progress on the statement's own quantity (in the abc sense), while the opposite reading holds that a bound on E(X) does not move the conjectured value and so counts for nothing.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The Captain Sude X announcement text and any authors' statement on how the argument was found and whether an AI system produced it. (2) A readable copy of Meng's eScholarship paper, including its AI-use statement and the abstract. (3) A written expert assessment of the repository's Lean statement and its use of Mangerel's published bound, and of the English paper. (4) Zhao's convention on whether 2 is counted in E(X), and any remark in the paper on the conjecture. (5) For the Deligiannis and Agama claims, the hypotheses and the full threshold argument.

event.what_happened: Genheng Zhao, 'The exceptional set of Goldbach problem and Linnik's constant', arXiv:2511.05631 (v1 7 Nov 2025; v2 23 Jan 2026, current). Proves E(X) = O(X^{7/10}), with ineffective implied constant, where E(X) is the number of even integers below X that are not a sum of two primes. The method also gives P(q) = O(q^5) for the least prime in an arithmetic progression mod q. A search summary attributes the exponent 0.709 to the paper; the v2 abstract says 7/10. I did not open v1.
event.delivers: A power-saving upper bound on the exceptional-set counting function E(X), unconditional per the abstract, with ineffective constant. This moves a quantity the conjecture is about: the conjecture is equivalent to E(X) counting only the number 2 (if 2 is counted) or nothing (if it is not). I did not confirm the paper's convention on whether 2 is counted. The bound says nothing about whether E(X) reaches that conjectured value.
event.remains: Whether the exceptional set is as the conjecture says (empty, or {2}). A bound X^{7/10} with an ineffective constant does not reach any X where the set is known to be the conjectured one.
event.direction: Moves the exceptional-set bound toward the conjecture's expected picture (exceptions are sparse). Neither proves nor disproves the conjecture.

judgement.why: The statement is the binary conjecture for every even n > 2. The Liouville-valued results (Captain Sude, Meng, Mangerel, Krishnamoorthy, the multiples-of-4 repository) do not require prime summands, and Goldbach implies them rather than the reverse, so they are variants. Helfgott's ternary theorem is a variant too, and the 4·10^18 computation is instances. Zhao's O(X^{7/10}) exceptional-set bound moves a quantity the statement is about without settling it, so it is a bound: an unreviewed arXiv preprint with no specific doubt. Deligiannis's work is conditional on two unproven hypotheses, which makes it a reduction (none). The self-published full-proof claims show several F10 signals together (a landmark problem, no uptake, fringe venues, patch histories, fitted or missing arguments), so they are not_credible. Bournas withdrew his claim. Captain Sude's Liouville event gets 'generated' because a press relay attributes the statement that Astra found the proof to the author. That has no effect here because the event is a variant.
judgement.doubts: The Astra attribution for the Liouville result rests only on a press relay of an unreadable X post; the repository names no AI. Zhao's bound is unreviewed, and a search summary gave a different exponent (0.709) for v1. The dissertation's 'generated' role is self-declared, and the work settles nothing.
